mainTopic: Damage on another's property, an ox falling into a pit, who guards an ox brought into a yard, and payment for a miscarriage
overview: The amud opens with a ברייתא about two people who damage each other. From it the גמרא learns that when only one had permission to be there, he is פטור and the trespasser is חייב. Next comes the משנה's ox that fell into a pit and spoiled the water. רבא's ruling is first explained by treating the ox as a בור, but that does not fit רב, so the final version is different: the owner is חייב if the ox's body spoiled the water, and פטור if only its smell did, because that is גרמא. For the father or son killed in the pit, the גמרא asks why a תם pays כופר. רב, שמואל, and עולא each give a different answer. On the משנה about bringing an ox in with permission, רב rules like the תנא קמא and שמואל rules like רבי. A ברייתא about 'guard it' versus 'I will guard it' seems to split between the רבנן and רבי. רבי אלעזר, רבא, and רב פפא each resolve this differently. Finally a new משנה begins: an ox that causes a miscarriage is פטור from דמי ולדות, but a person pays, by comparing the woman's value before and after birth. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's comment continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A ברייתא about two people who damage each other
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that if two people were in a place with the same status (both with permission or both without) and directly damaged each other, both pay. If they only got hurt by bumping into each other, both are פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: If both were there with permission, or both were there without permission, and they damaged each other, they are liable. If they got hurt by each other, they are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to support the earlier ruling of רבא and רב פפא about a homeowner and someone who entered without permission. This step sets up the inference that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא separates two cases. In the first, they actively damaged each other, so both are חייב. In the second, they were damaged by each other by accident, like bumping, so both are פטור. The ברייתא only talks about two people who have the same status.
steps.confusionAlert: Watch the two verbs closely. הִזִּיקוּ means they did the damage, and they pay. הוּזְּקוּ means they just got hurt by bumping into each other, and nobody pays.

phrases.english: If both of them were there with permission
or both of them were there without permission,
and they damaged each other, they are liable.
If they got hurt by each other, they are exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁנֵיהֶם בִּרְשׁוּת אוֹ שְׁנֵיהֶם שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא as support for the ruling of רבא and רב פפא from before this section.
steps.raayaObject: The ruling of רבא and רב פפא: when one person had permission and the other did not, the one with permission is פטור and the one without permission is חייב.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about two people who damage each other

steps.title: Inference: with permission is exempt, without permission is liable
steps.stepSummary: From the ברייתא's wording, the גמרא infers the rule for mixed status: the one who had permission is פטור, and the one who entered without permission is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason both are liable is that both had the same status. But if one had permission and the other did not, the one with permission is exempt and the one without permission is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads a hidden rule out of the ברייתא. This completes the proof for רבא and רב פפא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא made a point of saying 'both with permission or both without.' That shows that when their status is mixed, the rule changes. The homeowner, who belongs there, is פטור if he damages the trespasser. The trespasser is חייב if he damages the homeowner.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason is that (introduces an inference from a precise detail)

steps.whatToRemember: When one person belongs in a place and the other is trespassing, the one who belongs there is פטור for damaging the trespasser, and the trespasser is חייב.

phrases.english: The reason is that both of them were there with permission
or both of them were there without permission;
but if one was there with permission
and the other was there without permission,
the one with permission is exempt,
and the one without permission is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the inference from the ברייתא quoted in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: The ruling of רבא and רב פפא about mixed permission
steps.raayaSupportSource: The precise wording 'both with permission or both without' in the ברייתא
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: With mixed status, the one who has permission is פטור and the trespasser is חייב.

steps.title: The משנה: an ox fell into a pit and spoiled the water
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: if an ox brought in without permission fell into the owner's pit and spoiled its water, the ox's owner is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it fell into a pit and spoiled its water, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. This sets up רבא's explanation, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה's case, the ox entered the courtyard without permission. It fell into the courtyard owner's pit and made the water foul. The ox's owner has to pay for the ruined water.

keyTerms.meaning: A pit (also one of the main categories of damage)

phrases.english: If it fell into a pit and spoiled its water, he is liable.
phrases.notes: The 'it' is the ox that came into the courtyard without permission, and the pit belongs to the courtyard owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic: the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner of an ox that fell into someone's pit and spoiled the water is חייב.

steps.title: רבא: liable only if the water was spoiled at the moment of the fall
steps.stepSummary: רבא limits the משנה. The owner pays only if the water was spoiled at the time of the fall. If it was spoiled afterward, for example by the dead body rotting, he is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: They taught this only when it spoiled the water at the time of the fall. But if it happened after the fall, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא narrows the משנה's ruling to one specific situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא separates spoiling that happens right as the ox falls from spoiling that happens later. The משנה's חיוב covers only the first case. The reason comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: They taught this only (a phrase that limits a ruling)
At the moment of the fall

phrases.english: Rava said: They taught this only
when it spoiled the water at the time of the fall,
but if it spoiled it after the fall, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the משנה quoted in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner is חייב only if the spoiling happened at the time of the fall, not afterward.

steps.title: The reason: the ox is a pit and the water counts as utensils
steps.stepSummary: After the fall, the ox lying in the water acts like a בור that does damage, and the water is treated like כלים. The rule is that the owner of a בור does not pay for damaged כלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? The ox becomes a 'pit' and the water counts as 'utensils,' and we never find that a pit makes someone liable for utensils.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבא exempts damage that happens after the fall, and answers with a rule from the laws of בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the ox is lying still in the water, it is no longer actively doing damage. It is like an obstacle, so it falls under the category of בור. The תורה exempts the owner of a בור for damage to כלים, so the spoiled water, which is treated like כלים, is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: We have not found (no such case exists)

phrases.english: What is the reason?
The ox counts as a 'pit' and the water as 'utensils,'
and we have not found a pit
for which one is liable for utensils.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? הָוֵי שׁוֹר בּוֹר וּמַיִם כֵּלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for רבא's limitation in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is the owner פטור when the water was spoiled after the fall?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The resting ox counts as a בור and the water as כלים, and the owner of a בור is never חייב for כלים.

steps.title: This works for שמואל but not for רב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects. Treating the ox as a בור works for שמואל, who says any obstacle is a בור. But רב says something only counts as a בור once the owner gives up ownership (הפקר). The owner never gave up the ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for שמואל, who says any obstacle is a pit. But according to רב, who says it is only a pit once he renounces ownership of it, what can be said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason given for רבא's ruling, saying it does not fit רב's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling the ox a בור depends on a מחלוקת. According to רב, an object a person still owns is not a בור. The ox's owner did not make it הפקר, so the explanation falls apart for רב.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well for (sets up a challenge)

phrases.english: This works well for Shmuel, who said:
Any obstacle is a pit.
But according to Rav, who said:
it is not a pit until he renounces ownership of it,
phrases.notes: רב literally just says 'until he renounces it'; the rest is filled in from what we know he holds.

phrases.english: what can be said?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ox counts as a בור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to רב, an object only becomes a בור once it is made הפקר. The ox was not made הפקר, so it cannot be a בור, and the exemption for כלים does not apply.

steps.title: A second version of רבא: its body versus its smell
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא replaces the first version of רבא's statement. The owner is חייב only when the ox's body spoiled the water. If only its smell spoiled the water, he is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said: רבא said: They taught this only when it spoiled the water with its body, but if it spoiled it with its smell, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the first version of רבא and gives a different version that does not depend on calling the ox a בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new line between חייב and פטור is not about timing. It is about how the water was spoiled. Physical contact with the body makes the owner חייב, while smell alone makes him פטור. This version works for רב too.

keyTerms.meaning: If it was said, this is how it was said (replaces an earlier version)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new ruling added to the first one. It replaces the first version of רבא, which was rejected in the step before.

phrases.english: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said:
Rava said: They taught this only
when it spoiled the water with its body,
but if it spoiled it with its smell, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא in step 6 by restating רבא's ruling differently.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Restating the original statement in a different form
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא separated spoiling at the moment of the fall from spoiling afterward, based on the ox counting as a בור.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא separated spoiling by the body from spoiling by the smell, which works for רב too.

steps.title: Smell is only indirect damage, so he is exempt
steps.stepSummary: Damage caused by smell is only גרמא, indirect causing, and a person is not חייב for גרמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? It is merely indirect causing, and one is not liable for merely indirect causing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reason behind רבא's second version and closes the topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the body itself fouls the water, the damage is direct. When only the smell spreads and spoils the water, the ox did not directly do the damage; it happened on its own. That is גרמא, and the owner is פטור for it.
steps.whatToRemember: In the final version, the ox's owner is חייב if its body spoiled the water. He is פטור if only the smell did, because that is only גרמא.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
It is merely indirect causing,
and for merely indirect causing one is not liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the second version of רבא in step 7.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Spoiling caused only by smell is גרמא, and a person is not חייב for גרמא.

steps.title: The משנה: the father or son was inside the pit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה. If the pit owner's father or son was in the pit and was killed by the falling ox, the ox's owner pays כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If his father or his son was inside the pit, the ox's owner pays the ransom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה about a person killed when the ox fell into the pit. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the case was about an ox spoiling water. Now a person died when the ox fell on him. The משנה rules that the owner pays כופר, the payment the תורה requires when an ox kills a person.

keyTerms.meaning: Ransom money an ox owner pays when his ox kills a person

phrases.english: If his father or his son was inside it,
phrases.notes: He means the pit owner's father or son was down in the pit when the ox fell in.

phrases.english: he pays the ransom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the spoiled-water case to the next line of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ox's owner pays כופר when the ox falls into a pit and kills a person inside

steps.title: Why pay ransom if the ox is a תם?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why כופר is paid. A תם ox does not pay כופר, and an ox that falls into a pit seems to be a תם.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why does he pay? Isn't this ox a תם?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה. An ox that has no history of this behavior is a תם, and a תם does not pay כופר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה requires כופר only from the owner of a מועד ox, one that has been warned about its behavior. Falling into a pit is not normal behavior, so this ox should be a תם. The question is how the משנה can make the owner pay כופר.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox with no history of this kind of damage

phrases.english: But why? Isn't it a תם!
phrases.notes: The תורה requires כופר only from the owner of a מועד ox (שמות 21:29-30).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling just quoted from the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the owner pays כופר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only a מועד pays כופר, and an ox that falls into a pit is a תם

steps.title: רב: the ox was a מועד for falling on people
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that the משנה is talking about an ox that is a מועד for falling on people in pits.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: We are dealing with an ox that is a מועד for falling on people in pits.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question by saying the ox in the משנה is a מועד, not a תם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ox has already done this several times, it is a מועד for this behavior. A מועד ox pays כופר, so the משנה's ruling makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox that has been warned because it did this kind of damage repeatedly

phrases.english: Rav said:
With one that is forewarned to fall on people
in pits, we are dealing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: בְּמוּעָד לִיפּוֹל עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם בְּבוֹרוֹת עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by redefining the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ox is a תם, so it should not pay כופר
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox is a מועד for falling on people in pits, so כופר is paid

steps.title: If it is a מועד, the ox should be put to death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to רב. If the ox is a מועד for falling on people, it killed on purpose and should be put to death, yet the משנה mentions only כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the ox deserves to be put to death!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's answer. If the ox kills people on purpose, it should be stoned, not just have its owner pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox that kills a person on purpose is stoned. An ox that is a מועד for falling on people is acting deliberately. So the משנה should have said the ox is killed, and it did not.

keyTerms.meaning: Deserving to be put to death

phrases.english: If so, it is liable to be killed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב's answer
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the ox is a מועד for falling on people
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A מועד ox that kills on purpose must be stoned, but the משנה does not say so

steps.title: רב יוסף: it fell while going for grass
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף explains that the ox saw grass at the edge of the pit and fell in. It did not mean to kill, so it is not put to death, but the owner still pays כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: The case is where it saw grass and fell.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף defends רב by describing exactly how the ox fell.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox has a pattern of falling into pits, so it is a מועד and its owner pays כופר. This time it was reaching for grass and had no intent to kill. Without intent, the ox is not stoned.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
Where it saw grass and fell.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: דַּחֲזָא יְרוֹקָא וּנְפַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection against רב
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A מועד ox that kills should be stoned
steps.terutzMaskana: It fell without intent to kill, so it is not stoned, but its owner pays כופר

steps.title: שמואל: the משנה follows רבי יוסי הגלילי
steps.stepSummary: שמואל gives a different answer. The ox really is a תם, and the משנה follows רבי יוסי הגלילי, who holds that a תם pays half כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: Whose opinion is this? It is רבי יוסי הגלילי, who says a תם pays half כופר.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the original question from step 10 in a completely different way. He accepts that the ox is a תם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב changed the case to a מועד. שמואל keeps the ox as a תם and says the משנה follows a תנא who holds that even a תם pays כופר, just half. So when the משנה says 'pays כופר,' it means half.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who holds that a תם pays half כופר

phrases.english: Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: הָא מַנִּי – רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי הִיא,
phrases.english: Whose is this? It is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili,
who says: a תם pays half a ransom.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: הָא מַנִּי – רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the question of step 10, different from רב's
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the משנה to a specific תנא
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי יוסי הגלילי a תם pays half כופר, and the משנה follows him

steps.title: עולא: רבי יוסי הגלילי together with רבי טרפון
steps.stepSummary: עולא agrees the משנה follows רבי יוסי הגלילי, but adds רבי טרפון's view. A תם that gores in the injured party's yard pays full damages, so here the owner pays full כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: It is רבי יוסי הגלילי, who holds like רבי טרפון. רבי טרפון says a קרן in the injured party's yard pays full damages. So too, here he pays full כופר.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא gives a third answer. He explains how the משנה can mean a full כופר even though the ox is a תם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל read 'pays כופר' as half כופר. עולא reads it as full כופר. Here the person killed is the pit owner's father or son, so the pit belongs to the victim's own family, which makes it like the injured party's own yard. רבי טרפון holds that a תם pays in full there, so the full כופר is paid.

keyTerms.meaning: The damage category of goring, damage done on purpose
The yard of the injured party

steps.whatToRemember: There are three answers to why a תם pays כופר here. רב says the ox was a מועד, and it fell going for grass, so it is not stoned. שמואל says the משנה follows רבי יוסי הגלילי, so half כופר is paid. עולא says it follows רבי יוסי הגלילי together with רבי טרפון, so full כופר is paid because this was the injured party's property.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל and עולא both agree the ox is a תם and both follow רבי יוסי הגלילי. Their only difference is whether the משנה means half כופר or full כופר.

phrases.english: Ulla said:
It is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili,
who holds like Rabbi Tarfon, who says:
Goring in the courtyard of the injured party,
he pays full damage.
phrases.notes: Normally a תם that gores pays only half. רבי טרפון says it pays in full in the injured party's yard.

phrases.english: So too, he pays a full ransom.
phrases.notes: The pit belongs to the victim's family, so it is like the injured party's own yard.

steps.triggerLanguage: עוּלָּא אָמַר: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי הִיא – דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי טַרְפוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to step 10. It agrees with שמואל on רבי יוסי הגלילי but adds רבי טרפון
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the משנה to a combination of two תנאים' views
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A תם pays at most half כופר
steps.terutzMaskana: Combining רבי יוסי הגלילי with רבי טרפון, a תם in the injured party's property pays full כופר

steps.title: Why does the משנה mention the father or son?
steps.stepSummary: The detail 'his father or his son was inside the pit' fits עולא's explanation, but it seems pointless according to שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for עולא that the משנה says 'his father or his son was in the pit.' But for שמואל, why only a father or son? Anyone else should be the same!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the two explanations from steps 14 and 15 against one detail in the משנה: the person in the pit was the pit owner's father or son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For עולא, the father or son matters. It makes the pit area count as the injured party's own property, so רבי טרפון's rule of full payment applies. For שמואל, a תם pays half כופר anywhere and to anyone, so naming the father or son seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted / it works well for (one side), sets up a challenge to the other side
Why specifically this case? (implies the detail is unnecessary)

phrases.english: Granted, according to עולא,
this explains why the משנה teaches:
'if his father or his son was inside it.'
phrases.notes: For עולא, the father or son makes it the injured side's own pit and yard, so the case fits רבי טרפון's rule.

phrases.english: But according to שמואל,
why specifically his father or his son?
Even another person would be the same!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the explanations of שמואל (step 14) and עולא (step 15) using a detail in the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's explanation that the משנה follows רבי יוסי הגלילי's half כופר for a תם.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If half כופר applies to anyone anywhere, the משנה's detail 'father or son' serves no purpose.

steps.title: The משנה describes the usual case
steps.stepSummary: The משנה mentions a father or son only because that is who is usually found in a family's pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is just describing the normal way things happen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל. The detail is not a legal requirement. It is just the typical situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the person inside a family's pit is a family member. So the משנה uses that common picture. Under שמואל, the same half כופר would be paid for anyone.

phrases.english: It teaches the usual way things happen.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against שמואל in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a detail as describing the typical case, not a legal condition
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The mention of father or son seemed to be a necessary legal detail.
steps.terutzMaskana: The detail just reflects the common case, so שמואל's explanation still stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Both שמואל and עולא can explain the משנה. For עולא, 'father or son' matters for the law. For שמואל, it is only the usual picture.

steps.title: רב and שמואל disagree whose view is the הלכה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about bringing an ox in with permission. רב rules like the תנא קמא, and שמואל rules like רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says that if he brought the ox in with permission, the yard owner is responsible. It was taught: רב said the הלכה follows the first תנא, and שמואל said the הלכה follows רבי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה and reports a disagreement about the final הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא says that giving permission alone makes the yard owner responsible. רבי says he is only responsible if he clearly agreed to guard. רב rules like the first view, and שמואל rules like רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces an אמורא dispute)
The first (unnamed) opinion in the משנה

phrases.english: 'And if he brought it in with permission,
the owner of the courtyard is liable, etc.'
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' points to the rest of the משנה, where רבי says the yard owner is only liable if he agreed to guard.

phrases.english: It was stated: רב said:
The הלכה follows the first תנא,
and שמואל said:
The הלכה follows רבי.
phrases.notes: 'רבי' alone means רבי יהודה הנשיא.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם הִכְנִיס בִּרְשׁוּת בַּעַל חָצֵר חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, moving on to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב rules like the תנא קמא, so permission alone creates responsibility. שמואל rules like רבי, so the yard owner needs to have agreed to guard.

steps.title: Who must guard decides who is responsible
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: 'Bring in your ox and guard it' puts the responsibility on the ox owner. 'I will guard it' puts it on the yard owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our Rabbis taught: If the yard owner said 'Bring in your ox and guard it,' then if the ox caused damage, its owner pays, and if the ox got hurt, the yard owner is exempt. If he said 'Bring in your ox and I will guard it,' then if the ox got hurt, the yard owner pays, and if it caused damage, the ox owner is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא showing how the exact words of the invitation decide who is responsible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the yard owner tells the ox owner to do the guarding, the ox owner stays responsible for what his ox does. The yard owner is not responsible for harm to the ox. If the yard owner takes on the guarding himself, he must pay if the ox is hurt, and the ox owner is not responsible for damage the ox causes.
steps.confusionAlert: In each case, 'liable' and 'exempt' refer to different people. In the first case, the ox owner is liable and the yard owner is exempt. In the second case, the yard owner is liable and the ox owner is exempt.

phrases.english: Our Rabbis taught:
'Bring in your ox and guard it':
if it caused damage, he is liable; if it was hurt, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: The ox owner pays for damage, and the yard owner doesn't pay if the ox gets hurt.

phrases.english: 'Bring in your ox and I will guard it':
if it was hurt, he is liable; if it caused damage, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: Now the yard owner pays if the ox is hurt, and the ox owner is free if it causes damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא about the same topic as the משנה: an ox brought into another person's courtyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever agrees to do the guarding carries the responsibility: either for damage the ox causes, or for harm done to the ox.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that responsibility in someone else's property can depend on the exact words used when giving permission.

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself: quoting the first case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא announces that the ברייתא is difficult on its own terms and quotes its רישא: 'Bring in your ox and guard it.' If the ox damages, its owner pays. If it gets hurt, the yard owner is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ברייתא itself is difficult. You said: 'Bring your ox in and guard it.' If the ox caused damage, its owner is liable. If it was injured, the yard owner is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge. It says the ברייתא contradicts itself and starts by quoting the first case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הא גופא קשיא' means the problem is inside the source itself, not with some other source. The גמרא quotes the רישא now so it can draw an inference from it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: This itself is difficult: the source contradicts itself
It caused damage (the ox damaged something)
It was damaged (the ox itself got hurt)

phrases.english: This itself is difficult:
phrases.notes: 'This' means the ברייתא we just learned in Step 19.

phrases.english: You said: 'Bring in your ox and guard it' —
if it caused damage, he is liable; if it was injured, he is exempt;
phrases.notes: The ox owner pays for damage his ox causes, and the yard owner doesn't pay if the ox gets hurt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the ברייתא quoted in Step 19 and begins showing an internal contradiction in it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The internal consistency of the ברייתא about guarding an ox brought into a חצר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רישא and סיפא will imply opposite rules for the unstated case, where nobody says who guards.

steps.title: From the first case: with no stated terms, the yard owner takes on the guarding
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from the רישא that the ox owner is responsible only because he was told 'guard it.' So with no stated terms, the yard owner would be responsible, because he silently accepts the guarding.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason the ox owner is liable and the yard owner is exempt is that he told him 'guard it.' This implies that with no stated terms, the yard owner is liable and the ox owner is exempt, because in an unstated case the yard owner accepts the guarding upon himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a דיוק (inference) from the רישא. If the yard owner had not said 'guard it,' he would be the responsible one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Why did the ברייתא need the words 'guard it'? It must be because without them, the default would be the opposite. So the רישא teaches that, by default, letting someone's ox in means you take on the guarding.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason: the only reason is…
An unstated case, where nothing was said

phrases.english: The reason is that he said to him 'guard it'

phrases.aramaic: דְּחַיָּיב בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר וּפָטוּר בַּעַל חָצֵר,
phrases.english: that the ox owner is liable and the yard owner is exempt,
but if nothing was specified —

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּיב בַּעַל חָצֵר וּפָטוּר בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר,
phrases.english: the yard owner is liable and the ox owner is exempt,
because when nothing is specified, he accepts the guarding upon himself.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the yard owner. Just by letting the ox in, he takes on watching it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the רישא quoted in Step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The default rule for an unstated case, as implied by the רישא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רישא implies that in an unstated case the yard owner accepts the guarding. This sets up a clash with the סיפא.

steps.title: Quoting the second case: 'I will guard it'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now quotes the סיפא: 'Bring in your ox and I will guard it.' If the ox gets hurt, the yard owner pays. If it damages, the ox owner is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now look at the סיפא: 'Bring your ox in and I will guard it.' If the ox was injured, the yard owner is liable. If it caused damage, the ox owner is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the second half of the contradiction by quoting the last case of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the yard owner openly promised to guard the ox, so he carries the responsibility. The גמרא quotes this case so it can draw an inference from it, just like it did with the רישא.

keyTerms.meaning: Now say the last part (look at the final case)

phrases.english: Now say the last clause:
'Bring in your ox and I will guard it' —
if it was injured, he is liable; if it caused damage, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: Now it flips: the yard owner pays if the ox gets hurt, and the ox owner doesn't pay if his ox damages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the רישא to the סיפא of the same ברייתא, to build the other side of the contradiction.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Quoted in order to draw an inference that will clash with the inference from the רישא.

steps.title: From the second case: with no stated terms, the yard owner does not take on the guarding
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from the סיפא that the yard owner is responsible only because he said 'I will guard it.' So with no stated terms, the ox owner would be responsible, because the yard owner does not accept the guarding. This directly contradicts the inference from the רישא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason the yard owner is liable and the ox owner is exempt is that he said 'and I will guard it.' This implies that with no stated terms, the ox owner is liable and the yard owner is exempt, because in an unstated case the yard owner does not accept the guarding upon himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the opposite inference from the סיפא. Now the two halves of the ברייתא clash about the unstated case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רישא implied that in silence the yard owner accepts the guarding. The סיפא implies that in silence he does not. One ברייתא cannot hold both, so the קשיא is now complete and waits for an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part and the last part of a source

steps.whatToRemember: רישא: 'guard it' was needed, so in silence the yard owner guards. סיפא: 'I will guard it' was needed, so in silence the yard owner does not guard. The ברייתא seems to contradict itself about the unstated case.
steps.confusionAlert: Neither case in the ברייתא is actually silent. The contradiction is only about the unstated case that each half implies.

phrases.english: The reason is that he said to him 'and I will guard it'

phrases.aramaic: הוּא דִּמְחַיֵּיב בַּעַל הֶחָצֵר וּפָטוּר בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר,
phrases.english: that the yard owner is liable and the ox owner is exempt,
but if nothing was specified —

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּיב בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר וּפָטוּר בַּעַל חָצֵר,
phrases.english: the ox owner is liable and the yard owner is exempt,
because when nothing is specified, he does not accept the guarding upon himself;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors Step 21's inference, but from the סיפא, and reaches the opposite result.
steps.kashyaTarget: The consistency between the רישא and סיפא of the ברייתא about the unstated case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רישא implies the yard owner accepts the guarding in silence. The סיפא implies he does not. Both cannot be true in one ברייתא.

steps.title: The latter clause matches the view of רבי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא names whose view the סיפא's inference matches: רבי, who says the yard owner is responsible only if he clearly accepts the guarding.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have arrived at the view of רבי, who says the homeowner is not responsible unless he takes on the guarding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the inference from the סיפא matches רבי's opinion. This sets up the full challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 23 we learned from the סיפא that with no stated terms, the yard owner does not take on the guarding. That is exactly רבי's position: the homeowner is responsible only once he clearly agrees to guard.

keyTerms.meaning: We have come to, meaning this matches the opinion of...
רבי יהודה הנשיא, who disagrees with the רבנן here
Guarding, the job of watching over something

phrases.english: We have arrived at Rabbi,
phrases.notes: This is רבי's opinion in the משנה, which disagrees with the רבנן about silent permission.

phrases.english: who says: unless he accepts upon himself the guarding,
the homeowner, to guard.
phrases.notes: Read it as: until the homeowner accepts the job of guarding. Only then is he responsible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names whose opinion the inference from the סיפא in Step 23 matches.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא's inference matches רבי, while the רישא's inference matched the רבנן.

steps.title: Can the first clause follow the רבנן and the latter clause follow רבי?
steps.stepSummary: The challenge in full: it seems the רישא follows the רבנן and the סיפא follows רבי. Can one ברייתא really be split like that?
steps.simpleTranslation: The first clause is the רבנן and the latter clause is רבי?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the problem in full. It would be strange for one ברייתא to follow two opposite opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רישא implied that with silent permission the yard owner takes on the guarding (the רבנן). The סיפא implied that he does not (רבי). Normally we assume a single ברייתא follows one consistent view, so this split needs an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a teaching
The latter clause of a teaching

phrases.english: The first clause is the Rabbis and the latter clause is Rabbi?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the two inferences into one sharp challenge.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One ברייתא should not switch between two opposite opinions partway through.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: The ברייתא is indeed split
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר accepts the split: the ברייתא is 'broken', and different authors taught its two halves.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: It is broken. Whoever taught this clause did not teach that clause.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers by simply agreeing that the ברייתא is split between two opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not try to make the two halves fit together. The רישא follows the רבנן and the סיפא follows רבי, so the challenge is answered by accepting it.

keyTerms.meaning: Broken: the teaching is split between two views

keyTerms.term: מִי שֶׁשָּׁנָה זוֹ לֹא שָׁנָה זוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: Whoever taught this did not teach that
The אמורא giving the first answer

steps.confusionAlert: רבי אלעזר is not saying the ברייתא is wrong. He is saying its two halves come from two different opinions.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said: It is broken,
phrases.notes: 'Broken' here means split in two: the ברייתא doesn't follow one opinion all the way through.

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁשָּׁנָה זוֹ לֹא שָׁנָה זוֹ.
phrases.english: whoever taught this did not teach that.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 25 by accepting that the ברייתא is split.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the split: two authors for the two clauses
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A single ברייתא must follow one opinion.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רישא follows the רבנן and the סיפא follows רבי.

steps.title: רבא: The whole ברייתא follows the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the whole ברייתא follows the רבנן. The סיפא says 'I will guard it' only to match the רישא's wording 'guard it'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The whole ברייתא is the רבנן. Since the first clause used 'guard it', the latter clause was taught with 'and I will guard it'.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second answer that keeps the ברייתא consistent, following the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא removes the inference from the סיפא. The words 'I will guard it' were not needed for the law; even with silent permission the yard owner would be responsible. The ברייתא used them only to match the wording of the רישא.

keyTerms.meaning: All of it, the whole teaching
Since it used... (it repeats a style only to keep the wording parallel)

phrases.english: Rava said: All of it is the Rabbis,
since the first clause used 'guard it',
the latter clause taught 'and I will guard it'.
phrases.notes: So these words are just for matching style. Don't learn anything from them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to Step 25 that keeps the whole ברייתא following one view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Removes an inference: the wording is there only to match the other clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'I will guard it' in the סיפא is needed, so silent permission would not make the yard owner responsible.
steps.terutzMaskana: The words are only for matching style, and the whole ברייתא follows the רבנן.

steps.title: רב פפא: The whole ברייתא follows רבי, together with רבי טרפון
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the whole ברייתא follows רבי, and that it also holds like רבי טרפון: goring (קרן) in the injured party's yard pays full damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The whole ברייתא is רבי. And it holds like רבי טרפון, who says goring in the injured party's yard pays full damages.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a third answer. Here the whole ברייתא follows רבי, and he brings in רבי טרפון's rule to explain the רישא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא already fits רבי. The problem was the רישא, which seemed to need 'guard it' to make the ox owner responsible. רב פפא says the רישא is not about whether the ox owner is responsible at all. It is about how much he pays, based on רבי טרפון's full-damages rule; the next step explains how.

keyTerms.meaning: Goring, the damage category for an ox that attacks
The yard of the injured party
The תנא who holds goring in the victim's yard pays in full

steps.confusionAlert: Normally an ox that is not known to gore (תם) pays only half damages for קרן. רבי טרפון's rule of full damages applies only when it gores in the injured party's yard.

phrases.aramaic: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: כּוּלַּהּ רַבִּי הִיא;
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: All of it is Rabbi;
and it holds like Rabbi Tarfon,
who says: goring in the yard of the injured party,
he pays full damages.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: כּוּלַּהּ רַבִּי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to Step 25, the opposite of רבא's: everything follows רבי.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the רישא a new meaning using another תנא's rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Guard it' in the רישא is what makes the ox owner responsible at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Guard it' affects how much the ox owner pays, using רבי טרפון's full-damages rule.

steps.title: Saying 'guard it' gives the ox owner no place in the yard
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains: by saying 'guard it', the yard owner gives the ox owner no share of the yard. So if the ox gores, it is goring in the injured party's yard, which pays full damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore, if he said to him 'guard it', he is not giving him a place in the yard. So it is goring in the injured party's yard, and that pays full damages.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא finishes his answer by showing exactly what 'guard it' teaches in the רישא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Guard it' shows the yard owner is not giving the ox owner any rights in the yard; the yard still belongs fully to the yard owner. So goring there counts as goring in the injured party's yard, and by רבי טרפון's rule it pays full damages. This fits רבי, because the רישא is about the amount of payment, not about silently accepting the guarding.
steps.whatToRemember: Three answers to the split ברייתא: רבי אלעזר says it really is split between two views. רבא says it all follows the רבנן, and 'I will guard it' only matches the wording. רב פפא says it all follows רבי, and 'guard it' teaches full damages for goring in the injured party's yard, as רבי טרפון holds.

phrases.english: Therefore, if he said to him 'guard it',
phrases.notes: The yard owner is speaking to the ox owner.

phrases.english: he is not giving him a place in the yard,
and so it is goring in the yard of the injured party,

phrases.aramaic: וְקֶרֶן בַּחֲצַר הַנִּיזָּק מְשַׁלֵּם נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם.
phrases.english: and goring in the yard of the injured party pays full damages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבי טרפון's rule from Step 28 to the רישא's wording 'guard it'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the case: no rights in the yard were given
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Guard it' is what creates the ox owner's responsibility.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Guard it' means no place in the yard was given, so goring there pays full damages.

steps.title: Without 'guard it', the yard becomes shared and goring pays half
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא finishes his explanation. If the yard owner did not say 'guard it', he gave the ox owner a share of the yard. It becomes a partners' yard, where קרן pays only חצי נזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he did not say 'guard it', he gave the ox owner ownership of a spot in the yard. So it becomes a partners' yard, and goring in a partners' yard pays only half damages.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains the other half of the ברייתא: what happens when the yard owner just lets the ox in without saying 'guard it'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 29, saying 'guard it' meant the ox owner got no share of the yard, so goring paid full damages like רבי טרפון. Here, simply giving permission means the ox owner gets a share. The yard counts as shared, and in a shared yard קרן pays only half. Now both halves of the ברייתא fit רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: He certainly gave him ownership (here, a right to a spot in the yard)
A yard owned by partners, a shared yard
Goring, the category of damage where an ox harms on purpose
Half the cost of the damage

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב פפא, everything depends on the words 'guard it'. If he said them, the yard stays the injured party's alone and goring pays full. If he did not, the yard becomes shared and goring pays half.

phrases.english: If he did not say to him 'guard it'
phrases.notes: This is the yard owner speaking to the ox owner, just giving permission to bring the ox in.

phrases.english: he has given him ownership of a place in the yard
and it becomes a yard of partners
and goring in a partners' yard
pays only half damages

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב פפא's explanation by giving the opposite case to step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case distinction: the words 'guard it' decide whether the yard is shared or not.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two halves of the ברייתא seemed to need different authors (רבנן and רבי).
steps.terutzMaskana: The whole ברייתא follows רבי (with רבי טרפון). Without 'guard it' the yard is shared and goring pays half. With 'guard it' it is not shared and goring pays full.

steps.title: New משנה: an ox versus a person causing a miscarriage
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה begins. An ox that aimed at another and hit a pregnant woman, causing a miscarriage, is exempt from דמי ולדות. A person who did the same must pay דמי ולדות.
steps.simpleTranslation: An ox that was aiming at another ox, but hit a woman and she miscarried, is exempt from paying for the babies. But a person who was aiming at another person, but hit a woman and she miscarried, pays for the babies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new משנה. It compares an ox and a person who both accidentally cause a woman to miscarry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases the attacker aimed at someone else and hit the woman by accident. Even so, the משנה gives opposite rulings: the ox's owner is exempt from דמי ולדות, while a person must pay. The משנה states the rule here without explaining why.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין, 'our משנה', the start of a new משנה
Was aiming at, intending to hit
Payment for the unborn babies lost in a miscarriage
Exempt, does not have to pay

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. The ox's owner does NOT pay דמי ולדות, but the person DOES pay, even though both hit the woman by accident.

phrases.english: MISHNAH
An ox that was aiming at another
phrases.notes: For the ox, 'another' means another ox it wanted to gore.

phrases.english: and it struck the woman, and her children came out
phrases.notes: 'Her children came out' means she miscarried.

phrases.english: is exempt from payment for the babies
But a person who was aiming at another
and he struck the woman, and her children came out
pays for the babies

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, unconnected to the previous discussion of the yard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox that causes a miscarriage is exempt from דמי ולדות. A person who causes a miscarriage, even by accident, must pay דמי ולדות.

steps.title: How is the payment for the babies calculated?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks how the payment of דמי ולדות is figured out.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does he pay for the babies?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks a practical question: how do we put a money value on the lost babies? It is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 31 said the person must pay דמי ולדות but did not say how much. This question asks for the method of figuring out the amount.

phrases.english: How does he pay for the babies?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the details of the payment just required in step 31.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The method for calculating the amount of דמי ולדות.

steps.title: Compare the woman's value before and after birth
steps.stepSummary: The court appraises the woman's value before giving birth and after giving birth. The difference is the payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: We appraise the woman: how much she is worth before giving birth, and how much she is worth after giving birth.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers its own question. It gives the method: compare two appraisals of the woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The babies are not valued on their own. Instead, the court checks how much the woman was worth while still pregnant and how much she is worth after the birth. The gap between the two numbers is what the attacker pays.

phrases.english: We appraise the woman

phrases.aramaic: כַּמָּה הִיא יָפָה עַד שֶׁלֹּא יָלָדָה,
phrases.english: how much she is worth before she gave birth
and how much she is worth after she gave birth

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Appraise the woman before birth and after birth. The difference is the payment for the babies.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל begins his view
steps.stepSummary: The משנה introduces a statement by רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. His words continue in the next section.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said:
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the next move: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל is about to give his own opinion on how to calculate the payment. His actual words come in the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Right after the method given in step 33, a new speaker is introduced. This suggests he will add to or disagree with the calculation just described. We have to wait for the next section to see his words.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא, a leader of the generation, quoted in the משנה
'Our master', a special title for the head of the סנהדרין

phrases.english: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a second view on the calculation given in step 33.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduction only. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling follows in the next section.
